1.note: Hands like rivers: their generosity flows freely. The image is the author's; the sense is the usual one of an open hand.

2.note: בָּבוֹת are the apples of the eye (Zech 2:12, בָּבַת עֵינוֹ). The pair לְבָבוֹת וּבָבוֹת, hearts and eyes, is a rhyme.

3.he: כָּל לֵב הוֹמֶה. אֶל בִּין צָמֵא. / נָתַן עָלָיו מַיִם חֶיִּים
3.note: The first half-line, כָּל לֵב הוֹמֶה. אֶל בֵּין צָמֵא, is hard to construe word for word; it is translated by its sense: to every moaning heart and every thirsty one he gives living water.

4.he: כִּי בִלְשׁוֹנוֹ. וּבְהֶגְיוֹנוֹ / צִירֵי מָוֶת וּצְרִי חַיִּים
4.note: A pun: צִירֵי, pangs, and צֳרִי, balm. His words can wound and heal.

5.note: A pun: עֵרֶב רַב, the mixed multitude of Exodus 12:38, and עֲרָב, Arabic. Out of Arabic, the book would become a rabble.

6.he: אִם שְׁלָשׁ־אֵלֶּה לֹא יֵעָשֶׂה לָהּ וְיָצְאָה חִנָּם אֵין כָּסֶף
6.note: Exodus 21:7-11: a Hebrew handmaid whose master does not give her food, clothing and her conjugal right goes out free. Wisdom is sold as a handmaid, and leaves a master who does not honor her.

7.he: כֶּתֶר רֹאשׁוֹ דָּוִד וְחוֹתַם יְמִינוֹ שְׁלֹמֹה
7.note: The patron's line runs back to David and Solomon (line 322). The crown and the signet ring (the seal of Solomon) are their emblems.

8.note: נִיר is a lamp in 1 Kings 11:36 (נִיר לְדָוִד) and also a ploughed field; it rhymes with נֵר, lamp, in the half-line before.

9.he: כַּכָּתוּב: נִשְבַּע ה' לְדָוִד (תהלים קלב, ב)
9.note: The edition gives the reference as (תהלים קלב, ב), but the words נִשְׁבַּע ה' לְדָוִד are Psalm 132:11.

10.note: The abbreviations are read by their usual expansions: כג"ק as כבוד גדולת קדושת (his honor, the greatness of his holiness), שק"ל as שומרו צורו וחייהו (may his Rock keep him and give him life), זק"ל as זכר קדוש לברכה (of holy and blessed memory). The expansions are not certain.

11.he: נָשִׂיא אֲשֶׁר לוֹ כָּל נְשִׂיאֵי רוּם / נָתְנוּ שְׂרוֹךְ נַעֲלוֹ עֲלֵי לֶחְיָם
11.note: The image is uncertain. The princes bear his shoe-latchet on their cheeks, a sign of submission; or they put it at their jaws, as a bridle.

12.he: נִרְפָּא חֳלִי לִבָּם וְרָם שִׂיאָם / כִּי הוּא צֳרִי חֵילָם וְצִיר חָלְיָם
12.note: צִיר is both an envoy (Prov 13:17, צִיר אֱמוּנִים מַרְפֵּא, a faithful envoy is healing) and a pang; צֳרִי is balm. The line plays on all three.

13.he: כִּי הַגְּדֻלָּה בָנְתָה מִגְדָּל / לִשְׁמוֹ עֲלֵי כּוֹכְבֵי תְּלִי קַיָּם
13.note: תְּלִי is a constellation in medieval Hebrew astronomy (the name is the 'quiver' of Gen 27:3). The edition points קַיָּם, 'enduring', which the rhyme of the poem (־יָם) confirms; it is not כִּימָה, the Pleiades.

14.he: וּבַמֶּה יִתְרַצֶּה זֶה אֶל אֲדוֹנָיו הֲלֹא בְרָאשֵׁי
14.note: 1 Samuel 29:4: the Philistine lords say of David, 'with what should he reconcile himself to his master? should it not be with the heads of these men?' Here 'the heads' are the heads, the opening lines, of the patron's praises (line 353).

15.note: The speech begins without a lead-in, with the one word מְעוֹנִי, 'my dwelling', as if a line saying 'do not ask after my dwelling' were missing before it. The speaker promises to appear in every maḥberet: he is the book's hero, Ḥever the Kenite, though he is not named here.
